name: Bungalow
where: Mostly Ferry Green, with a few on the lower Common
hallmarks: Low porch across the front|Broad eaves|One story, sometimes with a dormer|Clapboard or brick porch piers
summary: The house that filled Ferry Green in the 1920s: a deep porch, a low roof, and rooms on one floor.
body:
Gablefen's bungalows are modest, not the West Coast craftsman type. The porch is the point: it faces the green, or the side yard, and it is where people actually sit.

Inside, the plan is usually a living room across the front, a dining room and kitchen behind, and two or three bedrooms off a short hall.

name: American Foursquare
where: West Common, almost street by street
hallmarks: Two-story cube|Pyramidal or hip roof|A full-width or offset porch|Four rooms to a floor
summary: The default house of West Common: a two-story cube under a hip roof, with a porch and an attic.
body:
You can date a Common block by the foursquares. They were ordered from catalogs and built by the same two contractors, which is why so many share a stair and a fireplace wall.

The attic often has a single dormer facing the street. A few have been opened into a fifth bedroom.

name: Mill cottage
where: Mill Reach, in short rows along the race
hallmarks: One and a half stories|A steep gable to the street|Brick or clapboard|A narrow lot and a small back yard
summary: The workers' house of the Reach: a steep gable, a narrow plan, and a yard that ends at the alley or the water.
body:
These were built in rows by the mill and later sold to the families who already lived in them. The rooms are smaller than a Common foursquare, and the stair is usually straight up from the front door.

A well-done cottage still has its original window proportions. A few have a later lean-to kitchen at the back.

name: Brick townhouse
where: The east side of Courthouse Square
hallmarks: Three stories of brick|A parapet, not a visible roof|A narrow front and a deep plan|Shared party walls
summary: A short brick row facing the courthouse lawn, with shops or a stoop at the sidewalk.
body:
Only one row was ever built. The ground floor of two houses is still a shop; the others were converted to dwellings all the way down.

Stairs are steep. Light comes from the street and from a small yard at the back.

name: Farmhouse
where: The edges of West Common and a few lots on Ridge Lane
hallmarks: Two stories|A gable roof|A porch along the long side|A later kitchen ell
summary: Older farmhouses that the town grew up around, now on in-town lots.
body:
A handful of houses predate the 1912 plat. They sit at odd angles to the later streets, which is how you spot them.

Rooms are bigger than a cottage and less regular than a foursquare. Most have a kitchen ell and a barn or garage at the back.

name: Cape
where: Ridge Lane and a few later lots on Ferry Green
hallmarks: One and a half stories|A steep gable with two dormers|A central door|Simple trim
summary: The post-war house of the ridge: a steep roof, two dormers, and a plan that can grow into the attic.
body:
Capes went up after the mill's last expansion, when the town needed houses faster than the Common could provide them.

The better ones have a full stair and two finished rooms under the roof. The simpler ones still have a pull-down attic.

name: Mid-century
where: The upper courts off Ridge Lane
hallmarks: A low, wide roof|A carport or an integrated garage|Windows in a band|One story, often on a slab
summary: A small group of ranches on the upper ridge, low to the ground, with a carport and a view.
body:
Only a dozen were built before the town stopped subdividing the ridge. They are the only houses in Gablefen with a carport as part of the original design.

Plans are open at the back, toward the view, and more closed to the street.
